info.album: I Feel Love (Remixed by Rollo / Sister Bliss and Masters At Work)

podcast.body: Produced by Giorgio Moroder, "I Feel Love" was an extraordinarily big hit in 1977. While rooted in disco, the song was distinctive for its robotic and futuristic sound, driven by Moroder's experimentation with new synthesizers. It proved to be extremely inspirational for musicians exploring synths and electronic music. "The album was disco, but it was different, robotic, futuristic, and those who were into experimenting with synths found it to be extremely inspirational."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: Released in 1977, this song is recognized as the first truly computerized and synthesized dance single. It was created with the help of producer Giorgio Moroder. While its disco elements were not universally liked, the pioneering use of synthesizers was appreciated, especially given that synthesizers were still very new at the time. "That's disco queen Donna Summer from 1977 with I Feel Love. That was the first truly computerized, slashed synthesized dance single, which she created with the help of producer George Eomeroder."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.body: The final track and lead-off single to the album *I Remember Yesterday*, this song reached number six on the Hot 100, becoming Summer's first Top 10 hit and gold single since "Love to Love You Baby," and her first number one hit in England. It is generally agreed to have single-handedly invented electronic dance music, being the first hit single with an entirely synthesized backing track, with only Donna Summer's voice as the organic element. Summer co-wrote its mantra-like lyrics and helped arrange its complex vocal melody, which was difficult to sing. The song was a smash in discos, particularly gay clubs, and influenced artists like Blondie, Human League, David Bowie, and Brian Eno. "I Feel Love is generally agreed to have single-handedly invented electronic dance music."

"algunas canciones de música disco americana eran muchísimo más cargadas de base rítmica pues como la hi-filov de Don Asammer pues se tras esta bajente europea como Jordi o Moroder."

podcast.body: This disco song, produced by Giorgio Moroder, featured a highly influential approach to using new keyboards. Its mechanical beat and programmed synthesizer pulse were considered high-tech and futuristic for 1977. "I feel love from 1977, produced by an Italian guy named Georgioma Rotor. Hugely influential approach to the use of these new keyboards."

podcast.body: This song was a significant disco breakthrough that presented "a completely different way of imagining pop music," evolving from the "Philly sound" towards synthesizer-heavy production. John Savage described it as obliterating "the tyranny of the clock" and creating "its own time." Donna Summer was already a star in Europe before its U.S. release, performing in stage productions and as a session singer. Producer Giorgio Moroder, a dance music trailblazer, heavily relied on the Moog synthesizer, taking inspiration from Kraftwerk. Despite its groundbreaking sound, neither Summer nor Moroder initially thought much of it as a single until Neil Bogart of Casablanca Records insisted. Released in July 1977, it became a worldwide hit, reaching number six on the Billboard Hot 100. In 2011, the Library of Congress added it to the National Recording Registry for its historical and cultural significance. "I Feel Love by Donna Summer was not just a disco breakthrough. It was a completely different way of imagining pop music."
